list.listitem: Hyponatremia represents a relative excess of water compared with sodium in the extracellular fluid; C the most common cause is syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone (SIADH).C
Among patients with severe hyponatremia (Na+ <115 mEq/L), 51.7% had altered sensorium, and 22.5% had seizures.C
Serum osmolality, urine osmolality, and urine sodium are helpful to establish the diagnosis.C
Treatment is based on the rapidity of onset of hyponatremia and presence or absence of symptoms.C
Carefully monitor during treatment to avoid osmotic demyelination syndrome; rate of correction should not be more than 0.5 mEq/L per hour or 10 to 12 mEq/L in 24 hours.B

Hyponatremia is defined as a serum sodium concentration less than 136 mEq/L (or mmol/L) (since sodium is univalent, 1 mEq/L = 1 mmol/L). It is further classified by sodium concentration as mild (130-135), moderate (125-129), and severe/profound (<125). It is also defined by time of development as acute (<48 hours) and chronic (>48 hours).

Hyponaremia is one of the most common disorders of fluid and electrolyte balance encountered in hospitalized patients. The prevalence in ICU patients is as high as 30%, and the prevalence at initial presentation to acute hospital care setting reported as high as 28%. The prevalence of hyponatremia in patients hospitalized for worsening heart failure reported as high as 27%; the prevalence in patients with cirrhosis and ascites as high as 57% in inpatients and 40% in outpatients.
It is common in nursing home residents (study found 53% of elderly nursing home residents had at least one episode of hyponatreamia in a 12-month period).
Studies have found a high proportion of iatrogenic or hospital-acquired hyponatremia, accounting for 38%-75% of hyponatremia seen in hospitals.
A meta-analysis found that hyponatremia is significantly associated with increased risk of overall mortality in hospitalized patients.
Whether hyponatremia is a direct cause of death or is simply a marker of severity of an underlying condition (like heart failure or cirrhosis) that is associated with death is not clear.
Another recent meta-analysis confirmed that hyponatremia is associated with a prolonged hospital stay and higher risk of readmission.
In the US, the direct annual cost of hyponatremia is estimated as between $1.6 and $3.6 billion.
See for a list of causes of hyponatremia.

Hyponatremia is classified as: Hypotonic hyponatremia (plasma osmolality < 280 mOsm/kg H2O); can be hypovolemic, euvolemic, or hypervolemic Hypovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia (renal sodium loss with water retention) Diuretic therapy (thiazides much more often than furosemide) Cerebral salt wasting (seen after subarachnoid hemorrhage, head injury, and neurosurgical procedures) Mineralocorticoid deficiency GI losses: protracted vomiting or diarrhea Third spacing
Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia SIADH (the most common cause of euvolemic hyponatremia) Nephrogenic Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuresis (due to 2 genetic mutations of the arginine vasopressin (AVP or ADH) receptor V2R (in the renal collecting ducts) leading to its activation and antidiuresis in the absence of AVP-V2R ligand binding), rare Isolated glucocorticoid deficiency (seen in pituitary disorders that impair normal ACTH secretion, leading to failure to suppress AVP, so resembling SIADH Hypothyroidism (rare, seen only in elderly with myedema coma. Due to decreased renal profusion and glomerular filtration rate due to decreased cardiac output and decreased peripheral vascular resistance, causing decreased effective blood volume and stimulation of AVP secretion Exercise-associated hypontremia (EAH). Most marathon runners with EAH are overhydrated due to excessive water drinking over the extended race time Low solute intake. Beer potomania (ingestion of large volumes of beer with little food), very-low-protein diets, and "tea and toast" diets Primary polydipsia
Hypervolemic hypotonic hyponatremia Heart failure. Here the nonosmotic release of AVP is the main cause of the water retention and hyponatremia Cirrhosis. Hyponatremia is common in advanced cirrhosis, but rarely without ascites. The major mechanism appears to be nonosmotic AVP stimulation Acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, and nephrotic syndrome. In acute kidney injury and chronic kidney disease, hyponatremia is due to water intake exceeding urine output and insensible losses In nephrotic syndrome, often serum albumin falls below 2g/dL, causing decreased intravascular volume and nonosmotic stimulation of AVP secreation causing hyponatremia
Isotonic hyponatremia (plasma osmolality 280-295 mOsm/kg H2O)—(1) hyperglycemia; (2) pseudohyponatremia (high concentrations of triglycerides, cholesterol, and protein) Hypertonic hyponatremia (plasma osmolality >295)—(1) severe hyperglycemia with dehydration; (2) mannitol; (3) hypertonic radiocontrast
The serum sodium concentration reflects the balance between total body water (TBW) and total body sodium.

Arginine vasopressin (AVP), the antidiuretic hormone (ADH), is released from the hypothalamus and promotes water reabsorption. This is normally stimulated by increased plasma osmolality via activation of osmoreceptors in the anterior hypothalamus and by decreased blood pressure or blood volume via activation of high- and low-pressure baroreceptors in the carotid sinus, aortic arch, carotid atria, and pulmonary veins.

AVP binds to the AVP V2 receptor subtype (V2R) in the renal collecting ducts and activates the signal transduction cascade resulting in antidiuresis. Hyponatremia usually is a state of low osmolality with relative excess of water compared with sodium in the extracellular fluid.

Inappropriately high ADH levels (inappropriate for the low serum osmolality) are the most common cause for hyponatremia (SIADH).The symptoms attributable to hyponatremia reflect neurologic dysfunction induced by cerebral edema. This causes increased intracranial presure, impaiored cerebral blood flow, and sometimes causing brainstem herrniation.
Runners should drink primarily when thirsty, with input no greater than 400 to 800 mL/h.C
Athletes should monitor weight, before and after exertion, as a guide to fluid consumption, with the goal to avoid weight gain.C
Among patients with severe hyponatremia (Na+ <115 mEq/L), 51.7% had altered sensorium, and 22.5% had seizures.C
Physical examination should focus on assessment of volume status (orthostatic blood pressures, skin turgor, edema) and neurological status.C
Serum osmolality, urine osmolality, urine sodium provide important information in the differential diagnosis of hyponatremia ().C

Most patients with mild hyponatremia are asymptomatic. Symptoms are more prominent when the decrease in serum sodium is large or occurs rapidly and usually reflect CNS dysfunction. Among patients with severe hyponatremia (Na+ <115 mEq/L), 51.7% had altered sensorium, and 22.5% had seizures.

Clinidal features of hyponatremia vary from mild, nonspecific to severe, life threatening. Symptoms of moderately severe brain edema are nausea without vomiting, confusion, and headache. Symptoms of severe brain edema are vomiting, cardiorespiratory distress, abnormal and deep somnolence, seizures, and coma (Glasgow Coma Scale <8).
Obtaining a detailed medication history is important, because many medications can cause hyponatremia. Table 7 in this reference lists the drugs that cause SIADH.
Physical examination should focus on evaluation of volume status (skin turgor, jugular venous pressure, heart rate, and orthostatic blood pressures) and neurological status.
In endurance athletic events weight gain during exercise can suggest hyponatremia.

Since direct measurement of intravascular volume is difficult, it is estimated clinically from the history, physical examination, and laboratory findings. Obtain a history of vomiting or diarrhea. Orthostatic decreases in blood pressure and increases in pulse, dry mucous membranes, and decreased skin turgor suggest volume depletion. At-risk populations include nursing home patients, hospitalized patients, postoperative patients, marathon runners, and patients with AIDS or ARC.
First exclude the nonhypotonic causes of hyponatremia (hyperglycemia, high concentrations of tryglycerides, cholesterol, or proteins, mannitol, and hypertonic radiocontrast).

The next step in the assessment of hypotonic hyponatremia is to check serum osmolality. In normal subjects, sodium, glucose, and urea are the primary circulating solutes. The normal range is from 275 to 290 mOsm/kg H2O. Serum osmolality is expected to be low in hyponatremia, because sodium is the primary contributor to the osmolality. See for a suggested approach to hyponatremia.

Hyponatremia with normal osmolality can be seen in hyperproteinemia and hyperlipidemia. This represents a lab artifact, which is therefore known as "pseudohyponatremia," and is less of a problem with newer ion-selective electrodes.

Hyponatremia with elevated osmolality can be seen in severe hyperglycemia with dehydration, with administration of hypertonic mannitol, and administration of hypertonic radiocontrast. These contribute to hyponatremia by inducing water movement out of the cells into the extracelluar fluid compartment.

If a hypoosmolar state is confirmed, the next step is to determine whether acute (<48 hours) or severe symptoms are present (nausea, malaise, headache, lethargy, obtundation, seizures, coma, respiratory arrest). If yes, immediate treatment with hypertonic saline should be considered.

If no, then determine whether the ability of the kidneys to dilute the urine is intact by measuring urine osmolality. The normal response of the kidney to a hypoosmolar state is to excrete maximally dilute urine, and urine osmolality is usually <100 mOsm/kg. If the urine is maximally dilute, it indicates that ADH secretion is appropriately suppressed and hyponatremia is unlikely to develop in this setting of an intact urine-diluting mechanism. However, it may develop in the rare instance of patients ingesting large amounts of water, low solute intake, and beer potomania.

In patients with hypoosmolar hyponatremia and inappropriately concentrated urine (urine osmolality >100 mOsm/kg), urine sodium concentration along with clinical volume assessment is useful to differentiate between hypovolemic and euvolemic hyponatremia. Typically, urine sodium concentration is <30 mEq/L in hypovolemia and is >30 mEq/L in SIADH (euvolemic hyponatremia).

Elevated blood urea nitrogen (BUN), creatinine, BUN/creatinine ratio, and uric acid suggest volume depletion. Urine spot sodium is <20 to 30 mmol/L in volume depletion, unless the kidney is the site of sodium loss.

Three caveats must be remembered about urine sodium: It will also be lowered by a low sodium diet. Recent use of a diuretic will increase urine sodium. Patients with CKD may be less able to reabsorb sodium and have impaired water excretion, so high urine sodium.
If urine sodium is <30 (low effective arterial blood volume) but clinically the extracellular fluid (ECF) volume is expanded, consider heart failure, liver cirrhosis, and nephrotic syndrome.
If urine sodium is <30 and clinically the ECF volume is contracted, consider diarrhea, vomiting, third spacing, and remote diuretics.
If urine sodium is >30 and the ECF volume is contracted, consider vomiting, primary adrenal insufficiency, renal salt wasting, and cerebral salt wasting.
If urine sodium is >30 and the ECF volume is normal, consider SIADH, secondary adrenal insufficiency, and possinly hypothyroidism.

Other tests: in patients in whom the diagnosis is not apparent after the initial evaluation, measurement of plasma uric acid, thyroid-stimulating hormone, and cortisol may be useful to establish the diagnosis.
In endurance athletic events, such as ultra-marathons and long-course triathalons, point of care sodium tests can be used to distinguish symptoms due to hyponatremia from dehydration.

Three novel markers being studied that may prove useful in the future in the evaluation of hyponatremia: Copeptin (C-terminal proarginine vasopressin), produced by enzymatic cleavageof the vasopressin prohormone. Apelin. Midregional proatrial natriuretic peptide (MR-proANP).

The need for treatment is guided by the rapidity of development of hyponatremia, its severity, and the presence or absence of symptoms.C

Prompt, controlled correction of sodium is indicated for acute symptomatic hyponatremia. The goal of treatment is to prevent seizures. Hypertonic saline may be continued until the patient is asymptomatic or until the sodium concentration reaches 118 to 120 mEq/L. Do not correct more than 10 to 12 mEq/L in 24 hours.C
Risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome is higher during correction of chronic hyponatremia but can be avoided by limiting the correction to less than 10 to 12 mEq/L in 24 hours.B
Vasopressin receptor antagonists have shown improvement in the serum sodium concentration in the short term in placebo-controlled trials.C
Treatment of hyponatremia should consider the rapidity of development of hyponatremia, its severity, and the presence or absence of symptoms.

A cutoff of 48 hours is used to differentiate between acute and chronic hyponatremia, because they may have different neurologic complications. Acute hyponatremia can cause cerebral edema, when the cells do not have enough time to adapt to the hypotonic excracellular environment. In chronic hyponatremia, the brain cells have adapted. Then treatment can cause an acute increase in extracellular tonicity causing osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS). So in patients with profound hyponatremia (<125 mmmol/L) it is helpful to know which complication to expect.

Those most at risk for acute hyponatremia are: postoperative patients, exercise (like marathon runners), use of "Ecstasy," and bladder irrigation (with glycine, sorbitol, or mannitol) during transurethral or hysteroscopic procedures.

Acute (<48 hours) symptomatic (typically CNS dysfunction) hyponatremia: initial goal is to increase serum sodium and to avoid seizures with hypertonic saline (3% sodium chloride) until the patient is asymptomatic or until sodium reaches 118 to 120 mEq/L. Total increase in 24 hours should not be more than 10 mEq/L. Several formulae () are available to estimate the sodium deficit in hypovolemic hyponatremia and to estimate the effect of 1 L IV fluids. However, the formulae rely on total body weight (TBW), and the clinical estimates of TBW are not completely accurate, so frequent measurements of serum Na MUST be performed in concert with the calculation used.
For severe hyponatremia, faster rates of sodium correction (>12 mEq/L) are associated with lower risks of death and acute neurologic events. No rates in this study exceeded 20mEq/L.
Severe symptoms include: headache, delerium, vomiting, seizures, coma, and neruogenic pulmonary edema.

Both current guidelines (United States and European) recommend treatment of patients with either acute hyponatremia or severe symptoms with boluses of 3% NaCl (100 ml over 10 minutes x 3 as needed (US) or 150 ml over 20 minutes x 2-3 as needed (European).

For patients with acute hyponatremia and mild to moderate symptoms (not defined), US guidelines recommend 3% NaCl infused at 0.5 to 2.0 mL/kg/hour. The European guidelines recommend for these patients the same bolus of 3% NaCl (150 ml over 20 minutes x 2-3 as needed) as for those with severe symptoms.

For patients with chronic hyponatremia and SIADH, both the US and European guidelines recommend fluid restriction as first-line treatment. Fluid restriction in SIADH provides a modest initial increase in sodium. Additional therapies are needed in many patients. For second-line treatment the US guidelines recommend demeclocycline, urea, or vaptan. For second-line treatment the European guidelines recommend urea or loop diuretics plus oral NaCl. They do not recommend vaptan, lithium, or demeclocycline.
For patients with chronic hypovolemic hyponatremia, the US guidelines recommend isotonic saline, the European guidelines recommend isotonic saline or balanced crystalloid solution.
For patients with chronic hypervolemic hyponatremia, the US guidelines recommend fluid restriction and vaptans. The European guidelines recommend fluid restrictions and recommends against vaptans.

US guidelines recommend a minimum of 4 to 8 mmol/L/day, and 4 to 6 mmol/L/day for patients at high risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome (serum sodium concentration <105 mmol/L, hypokalemia, alcoholism, malnutrition, or advanced liver disease). They recommend limits 10 to 12 mmol/L/day, 8 mmol/L/day for those at high risk of osmotic demyelination syndrome.
European guidelines recommend no minimum but a limit of 10 mmol/L/day.
The risk of sodium overcorrection is no different with either rapid intermittent bolus or slow continuous infusion of hypertonic saline for the management of symptomatic severe hyponatremia.

listitem.strong: Management of excessive correction of chronic hyponatremia:

list.listitem: US guidelines recommend that, if the starting serum sodium was >120 mmol/L, treatment of excessive correction is probably not necessary. If baseline serum sodium was <120, withhold the next dose of vaptan if the correction is >8 mmol/L during the first 24 hours. Consider administration of high-dose glucocorticoids (eg, dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours) for 24 to 48 hours following the excessive correction. Start re-lowering by giving desmopressin to prevent further water losses (2-4 micrograms every 8 hours parenterally). Replace water orally or as 5% dextrose in water IV 3 ml/kg/hour. Recheck serum sodium hourly and contnue therapy infusion until serum sodium is reduced to goal.

European guidelines recommend that, regardless of the baseline serum sodium, start relowering once the limit has been exceeded. Consult an expert regarding the correction. Re-lower with an infusion of electrolyte-free water (10 ml/kg) with or without 2 micrograms of desmopressin IV.
Vaptans such as tolvaptan block vasopressin type 2 receptors in renal collecting duct principal cells, causing aquaresis.
They represent targeted therapy for hyponatremia caused by excess vasopressin and have been shown to be very effective in SIADH, heart failure, and cirrhosis.
Both US and European guidelines state there is no place for vaptans in treatment of acute or severely symptomatic hyponatrekmia, when hypertonic saline is the treatment of choice.
Potential harms of vaptans include overcorrection and liver toxicity.
Both guidelines suggest that urea can be an alternative to vaptans for chronic hyponatremia due to SIADH.
It causes an osmotic diuresis of free water.
Hospitalize patients with hyponatremia who present with CNS symptoms, including mild cognitive dysfunction, representing a change from the patient's baseline.
Consult someone with vast experience in treating excessive correction of chronic hyponatremia if you do not have such experience.
Mortality rates as high as 18% to 30% are reported for hyponatremic patients. High mortality rates reflect the severity of underlying conditions and are not influenced by treatment of hyponatremia.

Hyponatremia prior to initiation of treatment is shown to be a predictor of cardiovascular mortality in severe congestive heart failure patients. Hyponatremic patients have a substantially shortened median survival compared with nonhyponatremic patients (164 days vs 373 days).
Water excretory capacity is impaired with aging, making the elderly population more vulnerable to hyponatremia.
Common in nursing home residents. Study found 53% of elderly nursing home residents had at least one episode of hyponatremia in a 12-month period.
Mild asymptomatic hyponatremia may influence gait and attention in elderly, resulting in a higher incidence of falls.
Hyponatremia occurs most commonly in children with hypovolemia due to gastrointestinal loss, who are managed by an excess intake of free water, in the setting of appropriately increased ADH.
Less commonly in children it is caused by renal salt wasting, when there is loss of sodium in excess of water in obstructive uropathy.
Also seen in skin losses of sodium in excess of water, like in cystic fibrosis.

Also seen in SIADH: causes in children include pulmonary and oncologic disorders, recent surgery, CNS injury or infection, endocrine disorders (adrenal insufficiency), certain medications (thiazide diuretics, chemotherapy drugs (cyclophosphamide, vincristine, and platinum-based agents), and antiepileptic drugs (valproate, carbamazepine, and oxcarbazepine)), and the rare nephrogenic symndrome of inappropriate antidiuresis (genetic mutation of the gene encoding the vasopressin type 2 receptor (AVPR2).

Intense exercise, like marathons, when accompanied by a high rate of fluid consumption, can cause hyponatremia, due to the high rate of fluid consumption along with the persistent secretion of ADH due to the initial hypovolemia.
Primary polydipsia.
Renal failure with the inability to excrete free water.
Effective arterial blood volume depletion: nephrotic syndome, cirrhosis, and heart failure.
Definition of chronic hyponatremia is different in children: in children it is serum sodium <135 for >24 hours (in adults it is >48 hours).

The rate of correction of hyponatrermia is also different in children: The recommended target correction rate is 6 to 8 mEq/L increase in plasma sodium in each 24-hour period. For adults the target is 4 to 8 mEq/L/day (4-6 mEq/L/day if high risk for ODS. For adults, after the first 24 hours, the recommemded limits are 10 to 12 mEq/L/day, 8 mEq/L/day for those at high risk of ODS. In both children and adults, too rapid correction can result in ODS.

Although hyponatremia affects all body cells, the clinical manifestations are mainly from the effects on brain cells. An acute (<48 hours), severe onset of hyponatremia can cause cerebral edema and sometimes death from brain hernation. Decreased serum tonicity causes water to cross the blood-brain barrier, increasing brain water content. By release of cellular solutes and water, equalizing intracellular and plasma osmolality, the brain adapts to serum hyponatremia. But brain adaptations that prevent cerebral edema make the brain vulnerable to injury if chronic (developing over >48 hours) hyponatremia is corrected too rapidly. This brain adaptation is complete in 48 hours.

The neurologic manifestations of this overly aggressive correction are called osmotic demyelination syndrome (ODS, previously know as central pontine myelinosis). Almost all patients who develop ODS present with serum sodium <120 mEq/L.
Factors that increase susceptibility to ODS: alcoholism, malnutrition, liver disease, and hypokalemia.
ODS symptoms usually occur 2 to 6 days after overly rapid elevation of serum sodium sodium.
One systematic review showed rapid correction of sodium levels in severe hyponatremia was NOT associated with a statistically significant increased risk of ODS.

ODS mainfestations are biphasic: initial decrease in symptoms as the hyponatremia is corrected, followed by a greadual onset of new neurologic findings (dysarthria, dysphagia, paraparesis, quadriparesis, behavioral disturbances, movement disorders, seizures, lethargy, confusion, disorientation, obtundation, and coma. Unfortunately some patients become "locked in", awake but unable to move (except their eyes) or communicate verbally.
ODS can cause permanent disability and death, but many patients, even those requiring mechanical ventillation, have full recovery of funtion.
Diagnosis: clinical picture as above then brain MRI. Brain MRI may not show signs for 4 weeks after onset.
Consult someone with vast experience in treating ODS, if you do not have such experience.

the optimal treatment is unclear. Data in humans is limited. Current recommendation is to relower the serum sodium to a level just below the maximum 48 hour target (to <16 mEq/L above the initial serum sodium). Relowering should be started as soon as possible after the diagnisis of ODS. Relowering regimens for ODS are the same as those for relowering in patients who have exceeded correction limits but have not yet developed ODS.
Slow correction and very slow correction of severe hyponatremia were associated with an increased risk of mortality and hospital length of stay compared to rapid correction.

Management of excessive correction of chronic hyponatremia: US guidelines recommend that, if the starting serum sodium was >120 mmol/L, treatment of excessive correction is probably not necessary. If baseline serum sodium was <120, withhold the next dose of vaptan if the correction is >8 mmol/L during the first 24 hours. Consider administration of high-dose glucocorticoids (eg, dexamethasone 4 mg every 6 hours) for 24 to 48 hours following the excessive correction. Start re-lowering by giving desmopressin to prevent further water losses (2-4 micrograms every 8 hours parenterally). Replace water orally or as 5% dextrose in water IV 3 ml/kg/hour. Recheck serum sodium hourly and contnue therapy infusion until serum sodium is reduced to goal. European guidelines recommend that, regardless of the baseline serum sodium, start relowering once the limit has been exceeded. Consult an expert regarding the correction. Re-lower with an infusion of electrolyte-free water (10 ml/kg) with or without 2 micrograms of desmopressin IV.

Supportive therapy: Recovery from seemingly hopeless defecits can occur, so supportive therapy should continue for at least 6-8 weeks before concluding that the defecits are irreversible. Since patients with severe ODS often develop aspiration pneumonia and respiratory failure, mechanical ventillator support is often needed.

cell.label: Hyponatremia. Exclude hyperglycemia and other causes of non-hypotonic hyponatremia.
Hypotonic hyponatremia. Acute or severe symptoms?
Consider immediate treatment with hypertonic saline.
Consider primary polydipsia, low solute intake, or beer potomania.

Low effective arterial blood volume. If ECF is expanded, consider heart failure, liver cirrhosis, or nephrotic syndrome. If ECF is contracted, consider diarrhea and vomiting, third spacing, or remote diuretics.
Consider diuretics as the cause, but still consider all other causes.

If ECF is contracted, consider vomiting, primary adrenal insufficiency, renal salt wasting, or cerebral salt wasting. If ECF is normal, consider SIADH, secondary adrenal insufficiency, or hypothyroidism. Consider occult diuretics as the cause.

listitem.strong: Hypotonic hyponatremia is further classified as:

list.listitem: ▪ Hypovolemic
▪ Euvolemic and
▪ Hypervolemic
Hypotonic hyponatremia (plasma osmolality <280 mOsm/kg H2O)

Hypovolemic hypotonic hyponatremia (renal sodium loss with water retention) ▪ Diuretic therapy (thiazides much more often than furosemide) ▪ Cerebral salt wasting (seen after subarachnoid hemorrhage, head injury, and neurosurgical procedures) ▪ Mineralocorticoid deficiency ▪ GI losses: Protracted vomiting or diarrhea ▪ Third spacing Euvolemic hypotonic hyponatremia SIADH (the most common cause of euvolemic hyponatremia) Nephrogenic Syndrome of Inappropriate Antidiuresis (due to 2 genetic mutations of the arginine vasopressin (AVP or ADH) receptor V2R (in the renal collecting ducts) leading to its activation and antidiuresis in the absence of AVP-V2R ligand binding), rare Isolated glucocorticoid deficiency (seen in pituitary disorders that impair normal ACTH secretion, leading to failure to suppress AVP, so resembling SIADH Hypothyroidism (rare, seen only in elderly with myedema coma. Due to decreased renal profusion and glomerular filtration rate due to decreased cardiac output and decreased peripheral vascular resistance, causing decreased effective blood volume and stimulation of AVP_secretion Exercise-associated hypontremia (EAH). Most marathon runners with EAH are overhydrated due to excessive water drinking over the extended race time Low solute intake. Beer potomania (ingestion of large volumes of beer with little food), very-low-protein diets, and "tea and toast" diets Primary polydipsia
Hypervolemic hypotonic hyponatremia ▪ Heart failure ▪ Cirrhosis ▪ Acute kidney injury, chronic kidney disease, and nephrotic syndrome
Isotonic hyponatremia (plasma osmolality 280-295 mOsm/kg H2O) ▪ Hyperglycemia and pseudohyponatremia ▪ Pleudohyponatremia (high concentrations of triglycerides,cholesterol, or protein)
Hypertonic hyponatremia (plasma osmolality >295 mOsm/kg H2O) ▪ Severe hyperglycemia with dehydration ▪ Mannitol ▪ Hypertonic radiocontrast

feature.caption: Formulas Used in Management of Hyponatremia.
feature.feature_body: Serum osmolality = [2 × Na (mEq/L)] + [BUN (mg/dL)]/2.8 + [Glucose (mg/dL)]/18 + [Ethanol]/4.6 Total body water (L) = (Body weight in kg) × (Correction factor) Correction factor is 0.6 for children and nonelderly men, 0.5 for elderly men and nonelderly women, and 0.45 for elderly women. Total sodium deficit (mEq) = [Total body water in L)] × [(Desired Na+) − (Actual Na+)] Na+ is in mEq/L. Sodium concentration in IV fluids is 0 mEq/L in 5% dextrose in water, 34 mEq/L in 0.2% saline, 77 mEq/L in 0.45% saline, 154 mEq/L in 0.9% saline, and 513 mEq/L in 3% saline Total liters IV fluids needed = Total Na+ deficit (mEq)/Na+ concentration in IV fluid (mEq/L) Serum Na+ change with 1 L of IVF = Na+ in IVF (mEq/L) − Serum Na+ (mEq/L)/Total body water (L) + 1 Example: A 60-kg young male presents with serum sodium of 116 mEq/L. Assuming a desired sodium level of 140 mEq/L, the sodium deficit = (60 × 0.6) × (140 − 116), which is a total sodium deficit of 864 mEq. Because 1 L of 0.9% saline has approximately 154 mEq of sodium, it would take 864/154 = 5.6 L of normal saline to increase the sodium to 140 mEq/L. However, the rate of correction should not exceed 0.5 mEq/L per hour or 12 mEq/L per 24 hours, so the 24 mEq/L rise in sodium should be achieved in no less than 48 hours. Thus, the rate of IV fluids is 5.6 L divided by 48 hours which is 116 mL/h of normal saline.
